Chapter Six: The Necessity of Solidarity—Moving Beyond Individualism
You know, there’s a quiet moment that shows up in every movement for change. It’s that instant when someone realizes, "I just can’t do this alone." Maybe it’s a worker, exhausted after another unfair shift, finally reaching out to a coworker. Or maybe it’s a parent, feeling overwhelmed by the challenges of raising a kid in a divided community, who finds a little comfort in a neighbor’s understanding smile.
In those moments, the old story of rugged individualism starts to crack. And in its place, something new begins to grow— solidarity.
For generations, a lot of us have been taught to put self-reliance on a pedestal. We love to tell stories about lone heroes—people who pull themselves up by their own bootstraps and conquer every obstacle through sheer willpower. But if you look a little closer, there’s a deeper truth that’s often hidden from sight. Real change—the kind that actually transforms lives and whole communities—almost always happens when people come together.
Picture a group of hospital workers. They’re frustrated about unsafe conditions, and they decide to speak up—not as individuals, but as a team. At first, the fear is real. What if they lose their jobs? What if management just ignores them? But as they start sharing their stories, something shifts. That heavy feeling of isolation starts to lift, and in its place, there’s a sense of shared purpose. Suddenly, they realize their struggles aren’t so unique after all—and by standing together, they actually have power.
Solidarity isn’t just about joining hands or chanting slogans. It’s about seeing that the same systems hurting one group, really end up hurting everyone. When wages are kept low for some folks, it gets easier to keep them low for all. When healthcare is denied to one community, the quality of care drops for everyone. Those lines that divide us—whether by race, class, or background—they aren’t natural. They’re drawn and redrawn by people who profit from keeping us apart.
Most of the time, we don’t even notice how often we’re encouraged to see others as competitors instead of allies. Think about the parent who worries that another child’s success means less for their own kid. Or the worker who’s afraid that helping a colleague will make them look weak. These habits are tough to shake, but they’re not set in stone. The moment you start seeing your own struggle in someone else’s, the walls begin to come down.
It becomes clear that solidarity isn’t just a strategy—it’s a necessity. In a society shaped by systems of exclusion, no one can truly thrive alone. The challenges are just too big, the forces too strong. But together, we can build something different. We can create communities where everyone is valued, where resources are shared, and where the promise of democracy actually means something.
The first step? It’s usually the hardest. It means reaching out, sharing your own vulnerability, and trusting that someone else will respond. But every single time someone chooses connection over isolation, the possibility for real change grows. The story of solidarity isn’t just about big movements or historic victories. It’s written in those everyday acts of courage and care—the kind that make a different world possible.
